intro: An adverb tells us how an action happens. Use a comparative adverb to compare two actions. Use a superlative adverb for the top one in a group.

sections.title: Short adverbs: -er and -est
sections.text: Fast, hard, high, low and long take -er and -est: faster/fastest and harder/hardest. For late, add -r and -st: later/latest. For early, change y to i: earlier/earliest.
examples: The library opened earliest on Monday.

sections.title: Most -ly adverbs: more and most
sections.text: Most adverbs ending in -ly use more and most: more carefully; most carefully. Do not add -er or -est to these adverbs. Early is different: earlier/earliest.
examples: The teacher spoke more clearly than before.

sections.title: Irregular forms and far
sections.text: Well → better → best. Badly → worse → worst. For damage, more badly and most badly can also be right. For distance, use farther/farthest or further/furthest.
examples: Jia answered the question better than before.
The rain damaged the paper sign most badly.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.text: Use faster, not more fast. Use more easily, not easilier. Use one pattern only.
examples: Our team finished faster than the other team.
Jia found the new bus stop more easily.

sections.title: Than, optional the, and hardly
sections.text: Use than after a comparative: more quickly than the other team. With a superlative adverb, the is often optional: She ran the fastest / She ran fastest. Hard means with effort. Hardly means almost not.
examples: Of the runners, Ming ran the fastest.
I could hardly hear the teacher.

miniCheck.explanation: Clearly ends in -ly, so use more clearly.

miniCheck.sentence: Of the three teams, the blue team played _____.
miniCheck.explanation: Well is irregular: well → better → best. The best is also correct here.

miniCheck.sentence: Of the three buses, Bus 2 arrived _____.
miniCheck.explanation: Early changes y to i: early → earlier → earliest. The earliest is also correct here.
